title: Balanced Forces
description: Apply Newton's First Law to analyze a system where two opposing forces cancel out — resulting in zero net force and no change in motion.
gap: Students confuse 'balanced forces' with 'no forces at all' — they think an object must be still for forces to be balanced, missing that constant-velocity motion also means net force = 0.
mission_brief: Mission: A tug-of-war robot on a frictionless surface is being pulled from both sides. Adjust the left and right force sliders until the robot stops accelerating. Observe how net force = 0 produces constant velocity — not necessarily stillness.
placement_q1_text: A box is sliding at constant speed across a frictionless surface. What is the net force on it?
placement_q1_options: No net force|A force in the direction of motion|A force opposing motion
placement_q2_text: Two teams pull a rope with equal force in opposite directions. What happens to the rope and why?
placement_q2_sample_answer: The rope doesn't move because the forces are balanced — net force is zero so there is no acceleration (Newton's First Law).
valerie_socratic_question: If the robot isn't accelerating right now, what does that tell you about the forces acting on it?

title: Magnetic Force & Distance
description: Investigate how magnetic force changes with distance using the inverse-square law — modeling real vector field magnitudes as separation increases.
gap: Students assume magnetic force decreases linearly with distance. They don't recognize the inverse-square relationship (F ∝ 1/r²) and underestimate how rapidly force drops off at greater distances.
mission_brief: Mission: Two magnets are fixed on a rail. Drag the movable magnet along the rail and watch the force vector arrows change in real time. Find the distance at which the force drops to 25% of its maximum — then predict what happens if you double that distance again.
placement_q1_text: If you double the distance between two magnets, what happens to the magnetic force between them?
placement_q1_options: It doubles|It stays the same|It drops to one-quarter|It drops to one-half
placement_q2_text: A student moves two bar magnets from 2 cm apart to 8 cm apart. Describe and explain the change in force.
placement_q2_sample_answer: The force drops to 1/16th of the original because magnetic force follows an inverse-square law — quadrupling the distance reduces the force by a factor of 4² = 16.
valerie_socratic_question: You just moved the magnet farther away. What pattern do you notice about how quickly the force is changing — is it slowing down or speeding up?

title: Newton's 2nd Law — F=ma
description: Plan and carry out an investigation proving that acceleration depends on both net force and mass — using deterministic kinematics (a = F/m; v += a·dt; pos += v·dt).
gap: Students treat F=ma as a formula to memorize rather than a causal relationship. They struggle to predict that doubling mass halves acceleration when force is constant, or that doubling force doubles acceleration when mass is fixed.
mission_brief: Mission: Load cargo onto a rocket sled and fire its thrusters on a frictionless track. Independently adjust thrust force and sled mass. Collect at least 4 data points to build an evidence-based F=ma graph. Your data must show both relationships to complete the mission.
physics_constant: a = F_net / m; v += a * dt; pos += v * dt
placement_q1_text: A 10 kg cart is pushed with 30 N of net force. What is its acceleration?
placement_q2_text: If you keep the force the same but triple the mass of the sled, what do you predict will happen to the acceleration? Use F=ma to justify your answer.
placement_q2_sample_answer: Acceleration will be one-third of the original. Since a = F/m, tripling m while holding F constant divides a by 3.
valerie_socratic_question: Your sled is moving really fast now. What combination of force and mass got you here — and how does that match what F=ma predicts?
